notes.front: In weight and balance, what is the datum?
notes.back: An imaginary vertical plane from which all horizontal measurements are taken for balance purposes, with the aircraft in level flight attitude.
notes.explanation: Every item’s location for a make and model is given in reference to it; the manufacturer chooses where it is.
notes.example: Like the zero mark on a tape measure laid along the fuselage: a fuel tank might be 60 inches behind it and a radio 90 inches ahead.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight & Balance Terminology”, p. 6-2
notes.evidence: The datum is an imaginary vertical plane from which all horizontal measurements are taken for balance purposes, with the aircraft in level flight attitude.

notes.front: What is the arm, and what do its plus and minus signs mean?
notes.back: The horizontal distance in inches from the datum to a point; plus means aft of the datum, minus means forward of it.
notes.explanation: An item exactly on the datum has an arm of zero, so its sign does not matter.
notes.example: Like house numbers counted from a crossroads: positive going one way down the street, negative going the other.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight & Balance Terminology”, p. 6-2
notes.evidence: The positive sign indicates an item is located aft of the datum, and the negative sign indicates an item is located forward of the datum.

notes.front: What is a moment in weight and balance, and in what unit is it expressed?
notes.back: Weight multiplied by its distance (arm) from the datum, expressed in inch-pounds (in-lb).
notes.explanation: For balance, the moments on each side of the balance point must be equal, as on a seesaw.
notes.example: Like a child on a seesaw: sitting farther from the pivot turns the same weight into a bigger moment.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight & Balance Terminology”, p. 6-2
notes.evidence: The weight is multiplied by the distance from the datum and the result is the moment, which is expressed in inch-pounds (in-lb)

notes.front: What is the centre of gravity (CG) of an aircraft?
notes.back: The point at which all its weight is concentrated and balanced, so the aircraft could be supported there.
notes.explanation: Suspended from this point, the aircraft would have no tendency to rotate nose up or nose down, because the nose-heavy and tail-heavy moments are equal.
notes.example: Like the one spot under a loaded wheelbarrow where it would balance on a single finger.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Center of Gravity (CG)”, p. 6-3
notes.evidence: The CG is the point at which all the weight of the aircraft is concentrated and balanced; therefore, the aircraft can be supported at that point (the CG).

notes.front: What is the maximum weight of an aircraft, and where is it found?
notes.back: The maximum authorised weight of the aircraft and its contents, given in the Aircraft Specifications or type certificate data sheet.
notes.explanation: For many aircraft it varies with the purpose and conditions of flight, such as normal or utility category.
notes.example: Like the gross vehicle weight plate on a lorry, which caps the truck plus its load.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Maximum Weight”, p. 6-3
notes.evidence: The maximum weight is the maximum authorized weight of the aircraft and its contents, and is indicated in the Aircraft Specifications or TCDS.

notes.front: What does the empty weight of an aircraft include?
notes.back: All operating equipment with a fixed location that is actually installed in the aircraft.
notes.explanation: That covers airframe, powerplant, required and optional equipment, fixed ballast, hydraulic fluid, and residual fuel and oil.
notes.example: Like weighing a car with its spare wheel and fitted radio but without driver, luggage or a tank of fuel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Empty Weight”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: The empty weight of an aircraft includes all operating equipment that has a fixed location and is actually installed in the aircraft.

notes.front: What is the empty weight centre of gravity (EWCG)?
notes.back: The point at which the aircraft balances in its empty weight condition.
notes.explanation: It combines empty weight and CG into one idea, and finding it is one of the most important reasons for weighing an aircraft.
notes.example: Like finding the balance point of an unloaded wheelbarrow before anything goes in it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Empty Weight Center of Gravity (EWCG)”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: The EWCG for an aircraft is the point at which it balances when it is in an empty weight condition.

notes.front: How is useful load found?
notes.back: Subtract the empty weight from the maximum allowable gross weight.
notes.explanation: An aircraft certificated in both normal and utility categories may have two useful loads listed.
notes.example: Like a van’s payload: the most it may weigh loaded, minus what it weighs empty.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Useful Load”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: To determine the useful load of an aircraft, subtract the empty weight from the maximum allowable gross weight.

notes.front: In weight and balance, what is minimum fuel?
notes.back: The fuel accounted for when a tank cannot be left empty in an adverse-loading check: the amount for 30 minutes of flight at cruise power.
notes.explanation: The aircraft cannot fly without fuel, so a tank behind the forward limit still carries this amount in the check.
notes.example: Like assuming a car always has at least half an hour’s fuel when you work out its lightest realistic load.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Minimum Fuel”, p. 6-5
notes.evidence: If the fuel tank is located behind the forward CG limit, it cannot be left empty because the aircraft cannot fly without fuel. In this case, an amount of fuel is accounted for, which is known as minimum fuel. Minimum fuel is the amount needed for 30 minutes of flight at cruise power.

notes.front: What is tare weight when weighing an aircraft?
notes.back: The weight of support equipment on the scales, such as a jack or chocks, which must be subtracted from the scale reading.
notes.explanation: The scale absorbs that equipment’s weight as well as the aircraft’s.
notes.example: Like the weight of the bowl you zero out before weighing flour on a kitchen scale.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Tare Weight”, p. 6-5
notes.evidence: Unfortunately, the scale is now absorbing the weight of the jack in addition to the weight of the airplane. This extra weight is known as tare weight and must be subtracted from the scale reading.

notes.front: On a loading graph, what is the moment index?
notes.back: The moment divided by 1,000.
notes.explanation: The loading graph turns each load item’s weight into its index number (moment value).
notes.example: Like quoting a price in thousands: 12.5 stands for 12,500.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Loading Graphs & CG Envelopes (Figure 6-43)”, p. 6-25
notes.evidence: Moment Index (Moment/1,000) Figure 6-43. Aircraft loading graph.

notes.front: Where does the weight and balance data needed to weigh an aircraft come from?
notes.back: The type certificate data sheet or Aircraft Specifications, furnished to anyone for every certificated aircraft.
notes.explanation: This information must be known before an aircraft can be properly weighed and its EWCG computed.
notes.example: Like a car maker’s published specification sheet, but official and available for every certificated type.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight and Balance Data”, p. 6-6
notes.evidence: Before an aircraft can be properly weighed and its EWCG computed, certain information must be known. This information is furnished by the FAA to anyone for every certificated aircraft in the TCDS or Aircraft Specifications.

notes.front: What is a spirit level, and how does it show level?
notes.back: A vial full of liquid except for a small air bubble; level is shown when the bubble is centred between the two black lines.
notes.explanation: An aircraft must be in level flight attitude before it can be weighed and reliable readings obtained.
notes.example: Like a carpenter’s level laid on the aircraft’s specified levelling screws.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Spirit Level”, p. 6-11
notes.evidence: Spirit levels consist of a vial full of liquid, except for a small air bubble. When the air bubble is centered between the two black lines, a level condition is indicated.

notes.front: What is a hydrometer used for in weight and balance?
notes.back: Checking the weight of fuel per gallon when an aircraft is weighed with fuel in its tanks.
notes.explanation: Its weighted glass tube floats at a level set by the fuel’s density, and the markings read in pounds per gallon.
notes.example: Like the float in a home-brewing kit, but graduated in pounds per gallon of fuel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Hydrometer”, p. 6-12
notes.evidence: When an aircraft is weighed with fuel in the tanks, the weight of fuel per gallon should be checked with a hydrometer.

notes.front: What are weighing points?
notes.back: The points where the aircraft’s weight is transferred to the scales: wheels, jacking points or special weighing points.
notes.explanation: The arm of each weighing point must be known to work out the empty weight centre of gravity.
notes.example: Like the three feet of a stool, each standing on its own bathroom scale.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weighing Points”, p. 6-14
notes.evidence: Some aircraft are not weighed with the wheels on the scales, but are weighed with the scales placed either at the jacking points or at special weighing points.

notes.front: Why must an aircraft be levelled before it is weighed?
notes.back: So it is in its level flight attitude and all components are at the correct distance from the datum.
notes.explanation: The level attitude, and how to check it, is given in the type certificate data sheet.
notes.example: Like standing a bookcase upright before measuring shelf heights from the floor.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Leveling the Aircraft”, p. 6-14
notes.evidence: When an aircraft is weighed, it must be in its level flight attitude so that all the components are at the correct distance from the datum.

notes.front: What is the CG range of an aircraft?
notes.back: The limits within which the aircraft must balance, an arm from the forward-most to the aft-most limit, usually in inches.
notes.explanation: The type certificate data sheet gives the limits, which may vary in a straight line between given weights.
notes.example: Like the safe zone on a seesaw where the pivot may sit and still let it balance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “CG Range”, p. 6-15
notes.evidence: The CG range for an aircraft is the limits within which the aircraft must balance. It is identified as a range and considered an arm extending from the forward most limit to the aft most limit usually expressed in inches.

notes.front: What is the operating CG range?
notes.back: The CG limits for the aircraft loaded and ready for flight; its CG must fall within them to fly legally.
notes.explanation: An aircraft that can operate in more than one category may have more than one set of limits.
notes.example: Like the safe loading zone painted on a lorry’s load bed, checked once the cargo is on.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Operating CG Range”, p. 6-16
notes.evidence: All aircraft have CG limits identified for the operational condition, with the aircraft loaded and ready for flight.

notes.front: What is temporary ballast?
notes.back: Lead bars, canvas bags of sand or lead shot carried, often in a baggage compartment, to adjust balance for certain flight conditions.
notes.explanation: The bags are marked with their weight and a warning that removing them requires a weight and balance check.
notes.example: Like a sandbag in the boot of a rear-wheel-drive car in winter, put in only when needed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Temporary Ballast”, p. 6-22
notes.evidence: Temporary ballast, in the form of lead bars, heavy canvas bags of sand, or lead shot, is often carried in the baggage compartments to adjust the balance for certain flight conditions.

notes.front: When is permanent ballast installed, and what is it usually made of?
notes.back: When a repair or alteration puts the CG outside its limit; usually lead blocks painted red and marked “Permanent Ballast – Do Not Remove”.
notes.explanation: It becomes part of the aircraft’s empty weight.
notes.example: Like a counterweight bolted to the back of a forklift, fixed for good.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Permanent Ballast”, p. 6-23
notes.evidence: If a repair or alteration causes the aircraft CG to fall outside of its limit, permanent ballast can be installed. Usually, permanent ballast is made of blocks of lead painted red and marked “Permanent Ballast–Do Not Remove.”

notes.front: What is the CG envelope?
notes.back: The shape formed when the forward and aft CG limits are plotted on a graph against weight.
notes.explanation: Its edges are graphic plots of the forward and aft limits.
notes.example: Like a fenced field on a chart: a loading plotted inside the fence is within limits.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “CG Range”, p. 6-15
notes.evidence: When graphically plotted, the CG limits form what is known as the CG envelope.

notes.front: What is the mean aerodynamic chord (MAC)?
notes.back: The average length of the chord (wing width) on a tapered, swept-back wing.
notes.explanation: On larger airplanes the CG and its range are usually given in relation to the wing’s width rather than only in inches.
notes.example: Like quoting a position as a fraction of a room’s average depth, when the room narrows from one end to the other.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight & Balance for Large Airplanes”, p. 6-28
notes.evidence: In relation to the aerodynamics of the wing, the average length of the chord on these tapered swept-back wings is known as the mean aerodynamic chord (MAC).

notes.front: Why does an extremely nose-heavy loading reduce efficiency?
notes.back: Higher than normal tail forces are needed for level flight; they add drag, needing more engine power and fuel flow.
notes.explanation: Improper loading reduces efficiency in ceiling, manoeuvrability, rate of climb, speed and fuel consumption.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Aircraft Weight & Balance”, p. 6-1
notes.evidence: If an airplane is loaded in such a way that it is extremely nose heavy, higher than normal forces are exerted at the tail to keep the airplane in level flight. The higher than normal forces at the tail create additional drag, which requires additional engine power and therefore additional fuel flow to maintain airspeed.

notes.front: What may happen if an aircraft is flown with its CG beyond its fore or aft limits?
notes.back: It may have insufficient stability, with resulting difficulty in controlling the aircraft.
notes.explanation: The handbook says “may”, and the warning covers both the forward and the aft limits.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Minimum Fuel”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: If the limits are exceeded and the aircraft is flown in this condition, it may lead to insufficient stability, with resulting difficulty in controlling the aircraft.

notes.front: What is an aircraft’s maximum weight based on?
notes.back: The lift the wings or rotors can provide under the operating conditions the aircraft is designed for.
notes.explanation: The handbook adds that taking off and landing at lower airspeeds is safer than at higher speeds.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Aircraft Weight & Balance”, p. 6-1
notes.evidence: The maximum weight of an aircraft is based on the amount of lift the wings or rotors can provide under the operating conditions for which the aircraft is designed.

notes.front: What must the weight and balance report issued at the factory include besides empty weight and CG?
notes.back: An equipment list showing the weights and moment arms of all required and optional equipment in the certificated empty weight.
notes.explanation: Every aircraft type certificated by the regulator gets this report as part of its required records before delivery.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Requirements for Aircraft Weighing”, p. 6-1
notes.evidence: The weight and balance report must include an equipment list showing weights and moment arms of all required and optional items of equipment included in the certificated empty weight.

notes.front: After which kinds of work must a new weight and balance report be created?
notes.back: Extensive repair, major alteration, or installation of new equipment such as a radio.
notes.explanation: The installer may weigh the aircraft or, knowing the exact weight and location of the new equipment, calculate the new report.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Requirements for Aircraft Weighing”, p. 6-1
notes.evidence: When an aircraft has undergone extensive repair, major alteration, or has new equipment installed, such as a radio or a global positioning system, a new weight and balance report must be created.

notes.front: Which two examples does the handbook give of aircraft that must be reweighed periodically, typically every 3 years?
notes.back: Part 135 air taxi and charter twins; and part 125 airplanes with 20 or more seats or at least 6,000 lb payload.
notes.explanation: Other aircraft may have no periodic requirement, though regular weighing is still good practice because aircraft tend to gain weight.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Requirements for Aircraft Weighing”, p. 6-2
notes.evidence: Some aircraft are required to be weighed and have their CG calculated on a periodic basis, typically every 3 years.

notes.front: Who chooses the datum, and where is it typically located?
notes.back: The manufacturer; typically the nose, the wing leading edge, a helicopter’s mast, or a set distance from a known point.
notes.explanation: Most modern helicopters, like airplanes, place it at the nose or a set distance ahead of it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight & Balance Terminology”, p. 6-2
notes.evidence: Typical locations for the datum are the aircraft nose, the leading edge of the wing, the helicopter’s mast, or a specified distance from a known point.

notes.front: Weight removed from forward of the datum produces what sign of moment?
notes.back: A positive moment (minus weight × minus arm).
notes.explanation: Like signs multiply to a positive answer; unlike signs to a negative one.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Center of Gravity (CG)”, p. 6-3
notes.evidence: Weight being removed forward of the datum produces a positive moment (−weight, −arm).

notes.front: In a four-column weight and balance table, how is the CG found?
notes.back: Total moment divided by total weight.
notes.explanation: The weight and moment columns are summed; the arm column is not, and its bottom figure is the CG.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Procedures for Weighing an Aircraft”, p. 6-6
notes.evidence: columns are summed, with the CG being equal to the total moment divided by the total weight. The arm column is not summed.

notes.front: Does choosing a different datum change where the CG physically is?
notes.back: No, provided all measurements are made from the same location.
notes.explanation: The CG’s arm number changes with the datum, but its physical position does not.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Datum Aft of the Main Wheels–Nosewheel Landing Gear”, p. 6-17
notes.evidence: It makes no difference where the datum is located if all measurements are made from the same location.

notes.front: What are residual fuel and oil, and are they part of empty weight?
notes.back: Fluids trapped in fuel lines, oil lines and tanks that do not normally drain out; yes, they must be included.
notes.explanation: The Aircraft Specifications or type certificate data sheet say which residual fluids count.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Empty Weight”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: Residual fuel and oil are the fluids that do not normally drain out because they are trapped in the fuel lines, oil lines, and tanks. They must be included in the aircraft’s empty weight.

notes.front: For most aircraft certified after {{c1::1978}}, the full capacity of the engine oil system is included in the empty weight.
notes.explanation: Older aircraft generally include only residual oil, which is why the date matters when preparing to weigh.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Empty Weight”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: For most aircraft certified after 1978, the full capacity of the engine oil system is also included in the empty weight.

notes.front: Why is the EWCG so important to all other weight and balance work?
notes.back: Loading for flight, equipment-change calculations and adverse checks all begin with the empty weight and EWCG.
notes.explanation: That crucial information is part of the aircraft weight and balance report.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Empty Weight Center of Gravity (EWCG)”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: All other weight and balance calculations, including loading the aircraft for flight, performing an equipment change calculation, and performing an adverse condition check, begin with knowing the empty weight and EWCG.

notes.front: What does useful load consist of?
notes.back: Fuel, other fluids not in empty weight, passengers, baggage, pilot, copilot and crew members.
notes.explanation: Whether engine oil counts depends on when the aircraft was certificated.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Useful Load”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: The useful load consists of fuel, any other fluids that are not part of empty weight, passengers, baggage, pilot, copilot, and crewmembers.

notes.front: Besides a jack on the scale, what are two other examples of tare weight?
notes.back: Wheel chocks placed on the scales, and ground locks left in place on retractable landing gear.
notes.explanation: Anything on the scale that is not part of the aircraft must be subtracted.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Tare Weight”, p. 6-5
notes.evidence: Other examples of tare weight are wheel chocks placed on the scales and ground locks left in place on retractable landing gear.

notes.front: A mechanic removes a rear seat that appears on the aircraft’s equipment list. Which records must they update?
notes.back: The weight and balance record, to show the new empty weight and EWCG, and the equipment list itself.
notes.explanation: The record and list must always match what is installed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight and Balance Data”, p. 6-7
notes.evidence: When an aircraft mechanic or repairman adds or removes any item on the equipment list, they must change the weight and balance record to indicate the new empty weight and EWCG, and the equipment list is revised to show what is installed.

notes.front: In what two ways can aircraft of all sizes be weighed?
notes.back: With top-of-jack load cells, or with platform scales.
notes.explanation: The choice depends on the operator’s needs, equipment on hand and the airframe manufacturer’s recommendations.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight and Balance Equipment”, p. 6-7
notes.evidence: Weighing GA aircraft, helicopters, turboprops, corporate jets, UAV/UAS, or transport category airliners can be accomplished in two ways: top of jack load cells and platform scales.

notes.front: A light airplane on portable platform scales sits slightly out of level. How can it be levelled?
notes.back: Only by deflating the tyres and landing gear struts as needed.
notes.explanation: Easy levelling is an important advantage of weighing on jacks with load cells.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Scales”, p. 6-8
notes.evidence: If an aircraft is weighed on platform scales, the only way to level the aircraft is to deflate tires and landing gear struts accordingly.

notes.front: What are the standard weights of aviation gasoline and jet fuel?
notes.back: Avgas 6.0 lb/gal; jet fuel 6.7 lb/gal.
notes.explanation: The values can vary dramatically between hot and cold days; when weighing with fuel aboard, the handbook says to check fuel with a hydrometer.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Hydrometer”, p. 6-12
notes.evidence: Although the standard weight for aviation gasoline (Avgas) is 6.0 lb/gal and jet fuel is 6.7 lb/gal, these values are not exact for all conditions.

notes.front: If it is impractical to drain the oil, the reservoir is filled to the specified level and the oil weight computed at {{c1::7.5}} lb/gal.
notes.explanation: Its weight and moment are then subtracted from the aircraft as weighed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Oil System”, p. 6-13
notes.evidence: If it is impractical to drain the oil, the reservoir can be filled to the specified level and the weight of the oil computed at 7.5 lb/gal.

notes.front: When weighing for empty weight, what are the three acceptable fuel conditions?
notes.back: Tanks and lines completely empty; tanks drained as the manufacturer specifies; or tanks completely full.
notes.explanation: In each case only residual (unusable) fuel should end up in the empty weight, by adding or subtracting fuel mathematically.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Fuel System”, p. 6-13
notes.evidence: When weighing an aircraft to determine its empty weight, only the weight of residual (unusable) fuel should be included. To ensure that only residual fuel is accounted for, the aircraft should be weighed in one of the following three conditions.

notes.front: Why must an aircraft never be weighed with its fuel tanks partially full?
notes.back: It would be impossible to determine exactly how much fuel to account for.
notes.explanation: Empty, drained or full tanks each give a known quantity to adjust for.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Fuel System”, p. 6-13
notes.evidence: Never weigh an aircraft with fuel tanks partially full, because it will be impossible to determine exactly how much fuel to account for.

notes.front: An older airplane certificated under Civil Air Regulations part 3 arrives for weighing with full engine oil. What must be done to find its empty weight?
notes.back: B) Drain the oil, or subtract its weight from the scale readings
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: full oil is part of its empty weight
B) Drain the oil, or subtract its weight from the scale readings
C) Add the oil capacity to the scale readings
D) Weigh it with the oil half drained
notes.choicesExplained: A describes most aircraft certified after 1978, not part 3 aircraft. C adds oil that is already on the scales. D leaves an unknown quantity.
notes.explanation: For these aircraft, engine oil is not part of empty weight, though undrainable oil remains in it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Oil System”, p. 6-13
notes.evidence: The empty weight for older aircraft certificated under the Civil Air Regulations (CAR) part 3 does not include the engine lubricating oil. The oil must be drained before the aircraft is weighed, or its weight must be subtracted from the scale readings to determine the empty weight.

notes.front: Which fluids are not part of an aircraft’s empty weight?
notes.back: Potable (drinkable) water, lavatory precharge water, and water for injection into the engines.
notes.explanation: Hydraulic and other reservoirs needed for normal operation should be full when weighing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Miscellaneous Fluids”, p. 6-14
notes.evidence: Fluids not considered to be part of the empty weight of the aircraft are potable (drinkable) water, lavatory precharge water, and water for injection into the engines.

notes.front: When an aircraft is weighed with its wheels on the scales, what should be done with the brakes, and why?
notes.back: Release them, to reduce the chance of incorrect readings from side loads on the scales.
notes.explanation: Care must also be taken to stop the aircraft falling or rolling off the scales.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weighing Points”, p. 6-14
notes.evidence: When weighing an aircraft with the wheels placed on the scales, release the brakes to reduce the possibility of incorrect readings caused by side loads on the scales.

notes.front: A tricycle airplane is weighed on three floor scales, and a second one on jacks. From which point is each weighing point’s arm measured?
notes.back: Wheels: the centre of each axle. Jacks: the centre of each jack pad.
notes.explanation: The arm of each weighing point is measured from that centre to the datum.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weighing Points”, p. 6-14
notes.evidence: the weight transfer to each scale happens through the center of the axle for each wheel. If an airplane is weighed while it is on jacks, the weight transfer happens through the center of the jack pad.

notes.front: Along which axis is levelling most important, and which aircraft must be level both ways?
notes.back: The longitudinal axis; helicopters must be level both longitudinally and laterally.
notes.explanation: On light fixed-wing airplanes lateral level is less critical, though a reasonable effort should still be made.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Leveling the Aircraft”, p. 6-14
notes.evidence: Helicopters must be level longitudinally and laterally when they are weighed. Accuracy in leveling all aircraft longitudinally cannot be overemphasized.

notes.front: When raising an aircraft on two wing jacks, what two precautions does the handbook give?
notes.back: Raise the jacks simultaneously, and keep the safety collars screwed down against the jack cylinders.
notes.explanation: The collars stop the aircraft tilting if a jack loses hydraulic pressure; raising together stops it slipping off.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Jacking the Aircraft”, p. 6-14
notes.evidence: When using two wing jacks, take special care to raise them simultaneously, so the aircraft does not slip off the jacks. As the jacks are raised, keep the safety collars screwed down against the jack cylinder to prevent the aircraft from tilting if one of the jacks should lose hydraulic pressure.

notes.front: If a data sheet lists an EWCG range and the aircraft’s EWCG falls within it, what follows?
notes.back: No legal loading can then put the loaded CG outside its range, so no adverse-loading check is needed.
notes.explanation: Most data sheets list the EWCG range as “None”, so a check is usually required.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Empty Weight Center of Gravity (EWCG) Range”, p. 6-15
notes.evidence: If the EWCG of an aircraft falls within the EWCG limits, it is impossible to legally load the aircraft so that its loaded CG falls outside of its allowable range.

notes.front: For a nosewheel airplane with the datum forward of the main wheels, what is the EWCG formula?
notes.back: CG = D − (F × L) ÷ W
notes.explanation: D is datum to main wheels, F the nosewheel weight, L the main-to-nose wheel distance and W the total weight.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “EWCG Formulas”, p. 6-16
notes.evidence: There are four possible conditions and formulas that relate the location of the CG to the datum.

notes.front: In a forward adverse-loaded CG check, which useful load items are loaded and which are left empty?
notes.back: Items in front of the forward CG limit are loaded; items behind it are left empty.
notes.explanation: If the fuel is behind the forward limit, minimum fuel is shown in the tank.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Adverse-Loaded CG Checks”, p. 6-20
notes.evidence: During a forward adverse-loaded CG check, all useful load items in front of the forward CG limit are loaded and all useful load items behind the forward CG limit are left empty.

notes.front: In an aft adverse-loaded CG check, which seat cannot be left empty even though it is forward of the aft limit?
notes.back: The pilot’s seat.
notes.explanation: All other useful load in front of the aft limit is left empty, and minimum fuel is shown if the tank is forward of it.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Adverse-Loaded CG Checks”, p. 6-20
notes.evidence: Even though the pilot’s seat will be in front of the aft CG limit, the pilot’s seat cannot be left empty. If the fuel tank is located forward of the aft CG limit, minimum fuel will be shown.

notes.front: After an equipment change, when may the new empty weight and EWCG be calculated rather than weighed?
notes.back: When the exact weight and arm of all the changes are known.
notes.explanation: Otherwise the aircraft is placed on scales and weighed.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Equipment Change & Aircraft Alteration”, p. 6-21
notes.evidence: The mathematical calculation is acceptable if the exact weight and arm of all the changes are known.

notes.front: Where is ballast usually placed, and why?
notes.back: As far aft or as far forward as possible, to bring the CG within limits using the least weight.
notes.explanation: The handbook notes that ballast placed farther from the affected limit needs less weight.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Ballast”, p. 6-22
notes.evidence: It is usually located as far aft or as far forward as possible to bring the CG within limits, while using a minimum amount of weight.

notes.front: What rules apply to temporary ballast in flight and at weighing?
notes.back: It must be secured so it cannot shift, must not exceed the compartment’s structural limits, and must be removed before weighing.
notes.explanation: Its bags are marked that removing them requires a weight and balance check.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Temporary Ballast”, p. 6-22
notes.evidence: Temporary ballast must be secured so it cannot shift its location in flight, and the structural limits of the baggage compartment must not be exceeded. All temporary ballast must be removed before the aircraft is weighed.

notes.front: What is the handbook’s temporary ballast formula?
notes.back: Ballast weight = total weight × distance needed to shift CG ÷ distance between ballast and desired CG.
notes.explanation: Shifting passengers or cargo is the other way to move a loaded CG into range.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Temporary Ballast Formula”, p. 6-22
notes.evidence: To determine the amount of temporary ballast needed, use this formula: Ballast weight = Total wt. × dist. needed to shift CG

notes.front: How does installing permanent ballast affect empty weight and useful load?
notes.back: It increases the empty weight and reduces the useful load.
notes.explanation: It must be attached so it cannot interfere with controls or be dislodged by manoeuvres or a rough landing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Permanent Ballast”, p. 6-23
notes.evidence: The installation of permanent ballast results in an increase in the aircraft empty weight, and it reduces the useful load.

notes.front: After the loading graph gives each item’s moment, how is the loaded CG checked on the CG envelope?
notes.back: Plot total weight against total moment; if the point falls inside the envelope, the CG is within limits.
notes.explanation: The graphs are prepared at original certification and usually kept in the flight manual or operating handbook.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Loading Graphs & CG Envelopes”, p. 6-24
notes.evidence: Where the horizontal and vertical plot lines intersect on the graph is the CG for the loaded aircraft. If the point where the plot lines intersect falls inside the CG envelope, the aircraft CG is within limits.

notes.front: How are lateral arms measured on a helicopter?
notes.back: From the butt line running nose to tail through the middle; right of it is positive, left is negative, facing forward.
notes.explanation: Helicopters have both longitudinal and lateral CG limits, so both weighing-point positions must be known.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Helicopter Weight & Balance”, p. 6-25
notes.evidence: Laterally, the arms are measured from the butt line, which is a line from the nose to the tail running through the middle of the helicopter. When facing forward, arms to the right of the butt line are positive; to the left they are negative.

notes.front: Why do weight-shift control aircraft and powered parachutes not have regulator-mandated weight and balance reports?
notes.back: They do not fall under the same regulations as certified airplanes and helicopters, so they have no type certificate data sheets.
notes.explanation: Weight and balance guidance is left to owners and the companies they work with.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight and Balance—Weight-Shift Control Aircraft and Powered Parachutes”, p. 6-26
notes.evidence: Weight-shift control aircraft and powered parachutes do not fall under the same Code of Federal Regulations that govern certified airplanes and helicopters and, therefore, do not have TCDS or the same type of FAA-mandated weight and balance reports.

notes.front: How is a CG in inches converted to percent of the mean aerodynamic chord?
notes.back: Subtract the leading edge of the MAC from the CG location, divide by the MAC length, and multiply by 100.
notes.explanation: Both the CG and the leading edge of the MAC are first identified in inches from the datum.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight & Balance for Large Airplanes”, p. 6-28
notes.evidence: Subtract LEMAC from the CG location. 4. Divide the difference by the length of the MAC. 5. Convert the result in decimals to a percentage by multiplying by 100.

notes.front: Where must the weight and balance report be when the aircraft is flown, and is there a required format?
notes.back: It must be in the aircraft; there is no required format.
notes.explanation: The report holds the current and accurate empty weight and EWCG, and is part of the aircraft’s permanent records.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight & Balance Records”, p. 6-31
notes.evidence: The weight and balance report must be in the aircraft when it is being flown. There is no required format for this report

notes.front: A 12 lb battery is installed 40 inches aft of the datum. What is its moment?
notes.explanation: Weight added aft of the datum gives a positive moment.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Center of Gravity (CG)”, p. 6-3
notes.evidence: Weight being added aft of the datum produces a positive moment (+weight, +arm).

notes.front: A 4 lb radio is removed from an arm of −20 inches. What is the moment change?
notes.back: A) +80 in-lb
notes.choices:
A) +80 in-lb
B) −80 in-lb
C) −24 in-lb
D) +16 in-lb
notes.choicesExplained: B gets the sign wrong: two negatives multiply to a positive. C adds weight and arm instead of multiplying. D subtracts them.
notes.explanation: Removed weight is negative and the arm is negative, so the product is positive.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Center of Gravity (CG)”, p. 6-3
notes.evidence: Weight being removed forward of the datum produces a positive moment (−weight, −arm).

notes.front: Items weigh 1,500 lb at +80 in, 170 lb at +90 in and 30 lb at +120 in. Where is their CG?
notes.explanation: Sum the moments and the weights, then divide total moment by total weight.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Procedures for Weighing an Aircraft”, p. 6-6
notes.evidence: columns are summed, with the CG being equal to the total moment divided by the total weight.

notes.front: An airplane has a maximum allowable gross weight of 2,400 lb and an empty weight of 1,520 lb. What is its useful load?
notes.explanation: Fuel, fluids not in empty weight, occupants and baggage must all fit within that figure.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Useful Load”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: To determine the useful load of an aircraft, subtract the empty weight from the maximum allowable gross weight.

notes.front: A main-wheel scale reads 812 lb. A 12 lb wheel chock sits on the scale with the wheel. What weight is used for that wheel?
notes.back: A) 800 lb
notes.choices:
A) 800 lb
B) 812 lb
C) 824 lb
D) 806 lb
notes.choicesExplained: C adds the tare instead of subtracting it. B ignores the tare. D subtracts only half of it.
notes.explanation: The chock is tare weight, so it is subtracted from the scale reading.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Tare Weight”, p. 6-5
notes.evidence: This extra weight is known as tare weight and must be subtracted from the scale reading.

notes.front: A piston engine has 180 maximum-except-takeoff horsepower. Using the simpler rule, what minimum fuel weight is used in an adverse-loading check?
notes.explanation: The handbook’s simpler method divides the maximum-except-takeoff horsepower by 2 to give pounds.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Minimum Fuel”, p. 6-5
notes.evidence: An even simpler way is to take the METO hp divided by 2, which is 100 pounds.

notes.front: The hangar is full and a supervisor suggests weighing the aircraft on scales outside on a breezy day. What is the concern?
notes.back: D) Wind over the surfaces can cause fluctuating or false scale readings
notes.choices:
A) There is no concern if the brakes are set
B) Sunlight changes the empty weight
C) Outdoor scales are always uncalibrated
D) Wind over the surfaces can cause fluctuating or false scale readings
notes.choicesExplained: B is not a stated effect. C overstates: nothing says outdoor scales are uncalibrated. A is wrong: brakes should be released on wheel scales, and wind still acts.
notes.explanation: The handbook says the aircraft should be weighed inside a hangar.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Preparing an Aircraft for Weighing”, p. 6-12
notes.evidence: The aircraft should be weighed inside a hangar where wind cannot blow over the surface and cause fluctuating or false scale readings.

notes.front: An aircraft arrives for weighing with its tanks about half full and no time to defuel fully. What should the technician do?
notes.back: C) Drain as specified, empty the tanks, or fill them before weighing
notes.choices:
A) Weigh it and estimate the fuel from the gauges
B) Weigh it and subtract half the tank capacity
C) Drain as specified, empty the tanks, or fill them before weighing
D) Weigh it as is and record the result as empty weight
notes.choicesExplained: A and B guess at an unknown quantity. D would count usable fuel in the empty weight.
notes.explanation: With partly full tanks, the exact fuel to account for cannot be determined.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Fuel System”, p. 6-13
notes.evidence: Never weigh an aircraft with fuel tanks partially full, because it will be impossible to determine exactly how much fuel to account for.

notes.front: Which of these is counted in an aircraft’s empty weight?
notes.back: B) Hydraulic fluid in the system
notes.choices:
A) Potable water in the galley tank
B) Hydraulic fluid in the system
C) Lavatory precharge water
D) Water for injection into the engines
notes.choicesExplained: A, C and D are the three fluids the handbook excludes from empty weight.
notes.explanation: Empty weight includes hydraulic fluid, and reservoirs should be full when weighing.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Empty Weight”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: It includes the weight of the airframe, powerplant, required equipment, optional or special equipment, fixed ballast, hydraulic fluid, and residual fuel and oil.

notes.front: An airplane with spring steel landing gear is jacked at the wheel for weighing. What should the technician expect?
notes.back: B) The gear will slide inward as weight comes off the tyre
notes.choices:
A) The gear will spread outward as weight comes off
B) The gear will slide inward as weight comes off the tyre
C) The gear will not move
D) The tyre will deflate
notes.choicesExplained: A is the opposite of the stated movement. C ignores the gear’s movement. D is not what happens when jacked.
notes.explanation: Care must also be taken to prevent the jack from tipping over.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Jacking the Aircraft”, p. 6-14
notes.evidence: If the aircraft has spring steel landing gear and it is jacked at the wheel, the landing gear will slide inward as the weight is taken off the tire. Care must be taken to prevent the jack from tipping over.

notes.front: A nosewheel airplane’s datum is 60 in ahead of the main wheels. The nosewheel reads 300 lb, the wheelbase is 50 in and total weight is 1,500 lb. Where is the EWCG?
notes.explanation: For a nosewheel airplane with the datum forward of the main wheels, CG = D − (F × L) ÷ W.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “EWCG Formulas”, p. 6-16
notes.evidence: Notice that the formula for each condition first determines the moment of the nose

notes.front: In a forward adverse-loaded check, the front seats and nose baggage are ahead of the forward CG limit, and the rear seats and fuel tank are behind it. What is loaded?
notes.back: C) Front seats and nose baggage at maximum, rear seats empty, minimum fuel
notes.choices:
A) Everything, at maximum
B) Rear seats and full fuel only
C) Front seats and nose baggage at maximum, rear seats empty, minimum fuel
D) Front seats only, with no fuel
notes.choicesExplained: A is not an adverse check. B is closer to an aft check. D forgets that fuel behind the limit is shown as minimum fuel.
notes.explanation: Items forward of the forward limit are loaded; those behind are left empty, except fuel at minimum.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Adverse-Loaded CG Checks”, p. 6-20
notes.evidence: If the fuel is located behind the forward CG limit, minimum fuel will be shown in the tank.

notes.front: Empty weight is 1,600 lb at +36.0 in. A 10 lb item at +60 in is removed and a 6 lb item is added at −10 in. What are the new empty weight and EWCG?
notes.explanation: Removed weight is entered as negative; each moment’s sign follows from the signs of weight and arm.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Equipment Change & Aircraft Alteration”, p. 6-21
notes.evidence: The weight of the equipment needs to be identified with a plus or minus to signify whether it is being installed or removed.

notes.front: A loaded airplane weighs 2,600 lb. Its aft CG limit is +100 in, but its CG is at +100.5 in. Ballast can go at +40 in. How much is needed?
notes.back: 2,600 × 0.5 ÷ 60 ≈ 21.7 lb, rounded up to 22 lb.
notes.explanation: The distance used is from the ballast to the desired CG, the aft limit: 100 − 40 = 60 in.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Temporary Ballast Formula”, p. 6-22
notes.evidence: To determine the amount of temporary ballast needed, use this formula: Ballast weight = Total wt. × dist. needed to shift CG

notes.front: After a panel upgrade, the EWCG falls just forward of the forward limit for every loading. Which fix does the handbook describe?
notes.back: C) Install lead blocks painted red and marked as permanent ballast
notes.choices:
A) Carry sandbags marked as temporary ballast on each flight
B) Leave it, since passengers will move the CG
C) Install lead blocks painted red and marked as permanent ballast
D) Change the datum
notes.choicesExplained: A suits certain flight conditions, not a lasting change from an alteration. B leaves an out-of-limit condition. D moves the reference, not the physical CG.
notes.explanation: Permanent ballast is for a repair or alteration that puts the CG outside its limit.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Permanent Ballast”, p. 6-23
notes.evidence: If a repair or alteration causes the aircraft CG to fall outside of its limit, permanent ballast can be installed.

notes.front: A pilot plots total weight and total moment on the CG envelope, and the point falls just outside the envelope line. What does it mean?
notes.back: C) The CG is not within limits for that loading
notes.choices:
A) The CG is within limits
B) Only the weight is too high
C) The CG is not within limits for that loading
D) The moment index needs rounding
notes.choicesExplained: A is true only for a point inside the envelope. B assumes the cause without checking. D changes nothing about the limits.
notes.explanation: A point inside the envelope means the CG is within limits.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Loading Graphs & CG Envelopes”, p. 6-24
notes.evidence: If the point where the plot lines intersect falls inside the CG envelope, the aircraft CG is within limits.

notes.front: The leading edge of the MAC is at 600 in, the MAC is 80 in long, and the CG is at 620 in. What is the CG in percent MAC?
notes.explanation: The CG is 20 in behind the leading edge of an 80 in chord, one quarter of the way back.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Weight & Balance for Large Airplanes”, p. 6-28
notes.evidence: imagine that the MAC on an airplane is 100", and the CG falls 20" behind the leading edge of the MAC. That means it falls one-fifth of the way back, or at 20 percent of the MAC.

notes.front: A data sheet lists an EWCG range. After an alteration, the new EWCG is inside it. Is an adverse-loading check needed?
notes.back: B) No, a legal loading cannot put the CG out of range
notes.choices:
A) Yes, always after any alteration
B) No, a legal loading cannot put the CG out of range
C) Only the aft check is needed
D) Only if the data sheet says “None”
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores the EWCG-range exception. C has no basis in the handbook. D reverses the logic: “None” is when a check is required.
notes.explanation: The handbook says no fore and aft adverse check is needed in this case.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Empty Weight Center of Gravity (EWCG) Range”, p. 6-15
notes.evidence: If the TCDS lists an EWCG range and, after a repair or alteration is completed, the EWCG falls within this range, then there is no need to compute a fore and aft check for adverse loading.

notes.front: An owner asks why weight above the maximum and a CG outside its limits both matter. Which pair of effects do the mechanic certification standards ask applicants to assess?
notes.back: C) Aerodynamic effect of CG outside limits, and aerodynamic and performance effects of excess weight
notes.choices:
A) Paint and upholstery wear
B) Tyre pressure and brake wear only
C) Aerodynamic effect of CG outside limits, and aerodynamic and performance effects of excess weight
D) Fuel grade and oil type
notes.choicesExplained: A, B and D are not the risk elements the standards list for weight and balance.
notes.explanation: Both are risk-management elements of the standards’ Weight and Balance task (Task C), so applicants must be able to assess them.
notes.source: FAA-S-ACS-1, Aviation Mechanic General, Airframe, and Powerplant Airman Certification Standards, Area of Operation I, Task C (Weight and Balance), AM.I.C.R4 and R5, p. 9
notes.evidence: Aerodynamic effect of CG that is forward or aft of CG limits. AM.I.C.R5 Aerodynamic and performance effects of weight in excess of limits.

notes.front: How does basic empty weight differ from licensed empty weight?
notes.back: Basic includes the full engine oil capacity; licensed includes only residual oil.
notes.explanation: Licensed empty weight generally concerns aircraft certified before 1978; basic empty weight matters most to maintenance.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Empty Weight”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: The term “basic empty weight” applies when the full capacity of the engine oil system is included in the value. The term “licensed empty weight” applies when only the weight of residual oil is included in the value

notes.front: How does payload differ from useful load?
notes.back: Payload is like useful load but does not include fuel.
notes.explanation: Both exclude the empty weight; only useful load counts the fuel.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Useful Load”, p. 6-4
notes.evidence: The payload of an aircraft is like the useful load, except it does not include fuel.

notes.front: Temporary or permanent ballast: which must be removed before the aircraft is weighed?
notes.back: Temporary ballast. Permanent ballast stays and becomes part of empty weight.
notes.explanation: Temporary ballast adjusts balance for certain flights; permanent ballast corrects a lasting CG problem after a repair or alteration.
notes.source: FAA-H-8083-30B, Aviation Maintenance Technician Handbook – General (2023), Chapter 6, Aircraft Weight & Balance, “Temporary Ballast”, p. 6-22
notes.evidence: All temporary ballast must be removed before the aircraft is weighed.
